# Using AI for Ind AS Research and Disclosure Checklists

> Use AI to find the right Ind AS paragraph, build disclosure checklists and compare peer disclosures. Never let it decide the accounting treatment. A CA’s method.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-10-using-ai-for-ind-as-research-and-disclosure-checklists
Last updated: 2026-11-10

CA insights · 2026-11-10 · 4 min read

Ind AS research is one of the places where AI is both most tempting and most dangerous. Tempting, because the standards are long and cross-referenced, and a good assistant can find the relevant paragraph in seconds. Dangerous, because a plausible answer about recognition or measurement can be completely wrong, and the error ends up in audited financial statements.

My rule is simple: AI may find, organise and compare. It may not decide the accounting.

## Who is on Ind AS

The [Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015](https://thc.nic.in/Central%20Governmental%20Rules/Companies%20%28Indian%20Accounting%20Standards%29%20Rules,2015.pdf) brought in Ind AS in phases. From accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2016: listed companies and companies in the process of listing with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, together with their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies. From 1 April 2017: the remaining listed companies and those in the process of listing, and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more but less than ₹500 crore, again with their group companies.

Voluntary adoption is irrevocable, and once a company applies Ind AS it continues even if it later falls below the thresholds. That leaves a long tail of mid-sized companies, and the CAs who work with them, who need reliable Ind AS research without a technical accounting team.

## Where AI is genuinely useful

Gartner’s [2025 AI in Finance survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) found knowledge management to be the most common finance AI use case, at 49% of adopters. Ind AS research is knowledge management with higher stakes.

- Finding the relevant standard and paragraphs for a fact pattern, as a starting point for reading the standard itself.
- Building a disclosure checklist for a specific company from the standards that apply to it, and marking which items are relevant to its transactions.
- Comparing a draft note with the checklist and flagging omissions.
- Comparing disclosures with peers. ICAI’s [CA GPT Industry Forum](https://icai.org/post/prc-icai-unveils-groundbreaking-ca-gpt-platform) integrated annual reports of about 5,000 listed companies for 2023-24 into its member platform, which makes this kind of benchmarking far quicker.
- Summarising changes between the previous year’s notes and this year’s draft.

## Where it must not go

Recognition, measurement, classification and judgement-heavy areas such as revenue from contracts with multiple obligations, leases, financial instruments, impairment and consolidation need a qualified person reading the standard and the facts. An assistant can describe what a standard says in general; it does not know your contract terms, and it will not reliably flag the exception that changes the answer.

I would also never accept an AI paragraph reference without opening the standard. References are where general-purpose tools fail most quietly: the paragraph exists but says something different, or belongs to a different standard.

## A research method that holds up

- Write the fact pattern first, in your own words, with the key contract terms.
- Ask the assistant for the relevant standards and paragraphs, not for the answer.
- Read those paragraphs in the official text, and any related guidance your firm relies on.
- Form the conclusion yourself, and write a short memo stating facts, analysis and conclusion.
- Keep the AI interaction in the file as supporting research, clearly labelled.

## Disclosure checklists: the best first use

If you want one place to start, make it the disclosure checklist. It is structured, it is easy to check against the standards, and an omission found by the checklist is cheap; an omission found by a regulator is not.

Treat the tool the way ICAI’s [SIA 240](https://internalaudit.icai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Comp-of-Stnd-on-Internal-Audit-26.pdf) asks internal auditors to treat any tool: validate its outputs against known results before relying on it, document how it was used, and apply professional judgement to everything it produces. Run last year’s approved financial statements through the checklist process first and see whether it finds what your reviewers found. Which assistant you use matters less than this discipline, though I compared the main options in [ChatGPT vs Copilot vs Gemini for a CA firm](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-05-chatgpt-vs-copilot-vs-gemini-how-a-ca-firm-in-india-should-choose-an-ai-assistant).

## Frequently asked questions

### Which companies must follow Ind AS?

Under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015: listed companies and those in the process of listing, unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more, and their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies, applied in phases from 1 April 2016 and 1 April 2017.

### Can AI decide an Ind AS accounting treatment?

No. It can help find relevant paragraphs and organise research, but recognition, measurement and classification decisions need a qualified person who has read the standard and the facts, documented in a memo.

### What is ICAI CA GPT?

ICAI’s AI platform for members, launched in July 2024 and free for members. In November 2024 ICAI added an Industry Forum with annual reports of about 5,000 listed companies for 2023-24.

### What is a good first AI use in financial reporting?

A disclosure checklist built from the standards that apply to the company, used to compare draft notes and flag omissions, validated first against a set of financial statements that has already been reviewed.

## Sources

# AI for GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C: What a CA Can Automate Before 31 December

> How a CA can use AI to prepare GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26, why filing before 30 November can cut off ITC, and what stays human.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-09-ai-for-gstr-9-and-gstr-9c-what-a-ca-can-automate-before-31-december
Last updated: 2026-11-09

CA insights · 2026-11-09 · 6 min read

How a CA can use AI to prepare GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26, why filing before 30 November can cut off ITC, and what stays human.

Key takeaways

- GSTR-9 for 2025-26 is due by 31 December 2026; turnover up to ₹2 crore is exempt under Notification No. 15/2025–Central Tax.
- Above ₹5 crore aggregate turnover, a self-certified GSTR-9C must be furnished with the annual return (rule 80(3)).
- Section 16(4) closes 2025-26 ITC on 30 November 2026 or on filing the annual return, whichever is earlier, so do not file GSTR-9 before the unclaimed-credit list is closed.
- From 2024-25 the portal highlights any override of a system-computed value in red, and the highlight stays after filing.
- Let AI build the tie-outs, Table 8A match, HSN split and 9C bridge; keep claims, liabilities and the signature with named people.

Every November the same two dates collide in a CA practice. Input tax credit for 2025-26 has to be taken by 30 November 2026, and the annual return for the same year is due on 31 December 2026. Clients want GSTR-9 done early. Before anyone hands the job to an AI tool or files in a hurry, look at how the two dates interact: filing early can shut a door you did not mean to shut.

This post is for CAs and finance leads preparing GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for 2025-26: what the law requires, where AI saves hours, and what stays with a person. It builds on my [GSTR-2B reconciliation method](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-how-to-use-claude-or-chatgpt-for-gstr-2b-reconciliation-a-ca-s-method); the annual return is where those monthly differences finally have to be explained.

## Who files what for 2025-26

Under [rule 80 of the CGST Rules](https://taxinformation.cbic.gov.in/content/html/tax_repository/gst/rules/cgst_rules/active/chapter8/rule80_v1.00.html), GSTR-9 is due by 31 December following the end of the financial year. A registered person whose aggregate turnover exceeds five crore rupees must also furnish GSTR-9C, a self-certified reconciliation statement, along with it. [Section 44(1) of the CGST Act](https://taxinformation.cbic.gov.in/content/html/tax_repository/gst/acts/2017_CGST_act/active/chapter9/section44_v1.00.html) describes that statement as reconciling the supplies declared in returns with the audited annual financial statement.

At the other end, [Notification No. 15/2025–Central Tax](https://egazette.gov.in/WriteReadData/2025/266213.pdf) of 17 September 2025 exempts registered persons whose aggregate turnover in a financial year is up to two crore rupees from filing the annual return, for 2024-25 onwards. So for 2025-26 the bands are simple: up to two crore, no GSTR-9; above two crore, GSTR-9; above five crore, GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C.

## The 30 November trap

[Section 16(4)](https://taxinformation.cbic.gov.in/content/html/tax_repository/gst/acts/2017_CGST_act/active/chapter5/section16_v1.00.html) says credit on an invoice or debit note cannot be taken after 30 November following the end of the financial year, *or* after furnishing the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. Read that twice. If a client files GSTR-9 for 2025-26 on 15 November, the window for any 2025-26 credit still sitting unclaimed closes on 15 November, not 30 November.

That is the first job I would give an AI tool this month: list every 2025-26 invoice that appears in GSTR-2B or the purchase register but has not been claimed in a GSTR-3B, with supplier, amount and month. A person decides what to claim before the deadline. Only then should anyone file the annual return.

## What changed on the portal

The [GST portal’s GSTR-9 manual](https://tutorial.gst.gov.in/userguide/returns/Manual_gstr9.htm) sets out several changes that matter for review:

- From 2023-24, Table 8A uses document-wise details from GSTR-2B. It includes only documents the supplier has actually filed, so not everything visible in GSTR-2B will appear there.
- From 2024-25, Table 6 has two new fields, A1 and A2, and some labels were revised.
- From 2024-25, any value that differs from the system-computed figure is highlighted in red as a warning, and the highlight stays after the return is filed.
- From 2024-25, you can download Table 12 HSN data from GSTR-1 and GSTR-1A, consolidated in the format Table 17 needs.

That red highlight matters. Every override of a system figure stays visible on the filed return, so each one needs a written reason in the working paper.

2025-26 also has a mid-year rate change. Most rate changes recommended at the [56th GST Council meeting](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2163555) took effect from 22 September 2025, so rate-wise and HSN-wise totals for the year combine two structures. Splitting turnover before and after that date is exactly the kind of mechanical sorting a tool does well.

## Where AI genuinely helps

- **Building the year-long tie-out.** Books against GSTR-1 against GSTR-3B, month by month, for outward supply and tax paid. The tool produces the table; every difference gets a reason column.
- **Table 8A against the books.** Matching the downloaded Table 8A document file to the purchase register, flagging supplier-not-filed, wrong GSTIN, duplicate and blocked-credit candidates.
- **HSN and rate splits.** Mapping item masters to HSN codes, consolidating Table 12 data for Table 17, and separating periods before and after 22 September 2025.
- **The 9C bridge.** Drafting the reconciliation from audited turnover to GST turnover: unbilled revenue, credit notes, advances, deemed supplies and non-GST income, each with the ledger it came from.

## Where judgement stays human

Four things should not be delegated. Whether to claim, reverse or pay on a difference is a tax position. Whether an unexplained gap is timing or under-declaration needs facts the ledger does not hold. Paying any additional liability through DRC-03 is a decision for the client and the partner. And GSTR-9C is self-certified, which means the client’s signatory owns every line, whoever drafted it.

The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) frames this as mapping where a system is used and managing the risk at that point. Here that means: the tool prepares, a person decides, and the decision is written down.

Decision rubric for GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C work. Evaluation framework only; adapt it to your practice. Not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Task | AI role | Minimum review gate | Stop if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unclaimed 2025-26 credit list | Automate | Manager decides each claim before 30 November | Anyone plans to file GSTR-9 before this list is closed |
| Books v GSTR-1 v GSTR-3B tie-out | Automate the comparison | Every difference above your threshold has a reason | Source files do not cover all twelve months |
| Table 8A against purchase register | Assist | Senior reviews blocked and ineligible credit flags | Eligibility is decided by keyword alone |
| HSN and pre/post 22 September split | Assist | Spot-check item mapping against invoices | The item master has no HSN field |
| Overrides of system-computed values | Draft reasons only | Manager approves each override in writing | An override has no evidence on file |
| GSTR-9C bridge to audited accounts | Assist (first draft) | Partner ties totals to signed financial statements | Accounts are not yet final |
| Additional liability, DRC-03, filing | Human only | Client signatory approves after partner review | The tool’s explanation is copied in as the conclusion |

## A workflow I would actually run

Start with one client above five crore. Export twelve months of GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-2B summaries, the Table 8A file, the HSN download and the trial balance. Strip customer and employee personal data first, and use a business AI plan whose retention terms a partner has read, as my [DPDP rubric for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric) sets out. A person writes the mapping rules; the tool builds the tables. Review the reasons, not the rows that agree.

The deliverable is a short evidence pack: the tie-outs, the unclaimed-credit decision log, every system-value override with its reason, the 9C bridge and the name of each reviewer. If the same team also files [AOC-4 and MGT-7](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-28-ai-for-aoc-4-and-mgt-7-filings-what-a-ca-can-automate-before-the-roc-deadline), reuse the master data. To roll it out across the client book, follow the [90-day pilot guide for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india).

## Monday-morning checklist

- Sort every GST client into three bands for 2025-26: up to two crore, above two crore, above five crore.
- Confirm all GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns for 2025-26 are filed for each GSTIN, so the annual return tile opens.
- Run the unclaimed-credit list and get decisions in before 30 November 2026. Do not file GSTR-9 before that.
- Download the Table 8A file and the HSN report for each GSTIN and store them with the working paper.
- Split rate-wise turnover at 22 September 2025.
- Agree who approves each override of a system-computed value, and who signs GSTR-9C.

To see where this sits among the other workflows in a practice, start from the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india). To find which compliance work is worth automating first, take the [free AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard), see the scoped [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), or [book a discovery call](https://pratikbajoria.com/#contact).

## Frequently asked questions

### Who must file GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26?

Registered persons whose aggregate turnover exceeds two crore rupees file GSTR-9 by 31 December 2026; those up to two crore are exempt under Notification No. 15/2025–Central Tax. Above five crore rupees, a self-certified GSTR-9C must also be furnished with the annual return under rule 80(3) of the CGST Rules.

### Does filing GSTR-9 early affect input tax credit?

Yes. Under section 16(4) of the CGST Act, credit for a year cannot be taken after 30 November following that year or after the annual return is furnished, whichever is earlier. Filing GSTR-9 for 2025-26 before 30 November 2026 closes the credit window on the filing date.

### Can AI prepare GSTR-9C?

AI can draft the reconciliation between audited turnover and GST returns and list the reasons for each difference. GSTR-9C is self-certified, so the client’s signatory owns every figure, and a CA or finance lead should review the bridge against the signed financial statements before filing.

# AI for Bank Statement Categorisation for Bookkeeping Clients in India

> Bank statement categorisation is the best first AI workflow for many bookkeeping practices: high volume, easy to check, low risk. How to set it up properly.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-06-ai-for-bank-statement-categorisation-for-bookkeeping-clients-in-india
Last updated: 2026-11-06

CA insights · 2026-11-06 · 4 min read

If a bookkeeping practice asks me where to start with AI, the answer is usually the bank statement. Every client has one, the volume is high, the categories repeat month after month, and every mistake is easy to see and fix before it reaches a return.

It is also unglamorous, which is part of the appeal. The aim is not a clever demo. It is getting a month of transactions into the right ledgers faster, with a person checking the parts that need checking.

## Why it is a good first workflow

It is also close to what finance teams already do with AI. Gartner’s [2025 survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) found error and anomaly detection among the three most common finance AI use cases.

- Volume: hundreds or thousands of lines per client per month, mostly repetitive.
- Checkability: each categorisation can be verified against the narration, the counterparty and the invoice.
- Low downstream risk if reviewed: errors are caught at the ledger stage, long before a return is filed.
- A learning loop: corrections made by the reviewer become rules for next month.

## Getting the data in cleanly

The weak point in most practices is not the categorisation; it is the input. PDFs, scanned statements and password-protected files waste more time than any classification error. Consent-based data sharing is changing that. India’s Account Aggregator ecosystem [crossed 500 million fulfilled consents in September 2026](https://sahamati.org.in/media-article/account-aggregator-crosses-500-million-consents-as-india-marks-5th-aa-foundation-day/), with more than 2.8 billion financial accounts enabled for sharing and over 1,100 regulated entities live, according to Sahamati, which the Reserve Bank recognised as the self-regulatory organisation for the ecosystem in June 2026.

Not every client or bookkeeping tool will use that route yet, but structured, consented feeds are the direction of travel. Where they are available, they remove a whole class of errors.

## A categorisation workflow that holds up

- Start with the client’s own chart of accounts and last year’s categorised data as the reference.
- Apply firm rules first, for known vendors, salary runs and tax payments, then let AI propose categories for the rest with a confidence level.
- Route low-confidence lines, round-figure transfers, cash withdrawals and related-party payments to a reviewer.
- Record every reviewer correction and turn recurring ones into rules.
- Reconcile the closing balance to the statement every month, without exception.

## Where the reviewer earns their fee

Some lines need judgement: whether a transfer is a loan, capital or a sale; whether a payment is personal; whether a receipt is income at all. Those decisions affect tax and should never be left to a model’s guess.

It also pays to look at the bank data the way the tax department does. The [Form 168 FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs) explain that banks are among the institutions whose reports feed the Annual Information Statement. Categorising transactions properly during the year makes the year-end comparison with the AIS much less painful.

## Mind where the books live

Under the new income-tax framework, the [Form 26 FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-26-faqs) point to Rule 46: where books of account are kept electronically they must remain accessible in India, with a daily backup on servers located in India, and the tax audit report asks for the server location. If a categorisation or bookkeeping tool stores client books, know where. If it processes data outside India, check whether that affects the client’s compliance before you rely on it.

If this is your first AI workflow, treat it as a pilot with a baseline and a decision date; my [90-day pilot playbook](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india) lists this as a good first candidate.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI categorise bank statements accurately?

For repetitive transactions with a good reference history, it can propose categories quickly. Accuracy depends on clean inputs and a reviewer who checks low-confidence, unusual and tax-sensitive lines and feeds corrections back as rules.

### What is the Account Aggregator framework?

It is India’s consent-based system for sharing financial data between regulated entities. According to Sahamati, it crossed 500 million fulfilled consents in September 2026, with more than 2.8 billion accounts enabled for sharing.

### Which transactions should a person always review?

Low-confidence suggestions, cash withdrawals, round-figure and related-party transfers, loans and capital movements, and anything that changes taxable income.

### Does it matter where bookkeeping software stores data?

Yes. Under Rule 46 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026, electronic books must remain accessible in India with a daily backup on India-located servers, and Form 26 asks for the server location.

## Sources

- [Income Tax Department: Form No. 26 FAQs (tax audit under section 63, Income-tax Act, 2025)](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-26-faqs)
- [Income Tax Department: Form No. 168 (Annual Information Statement) FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs)

# AI for Month-End Close in Indian Mid-Market Finance Teams

> Where AI shortens the month-end close for Indian mid-market finance teams: reconciliations, accrual support and variance commentary, with the controller signing off.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-05-ai-for-month-end-close-in-indian-mid-market-finance-teams
Last updated: 2026-11-05

Finance & compliance · 2026-11-05 · 4 min read

Ask a mid-market finance team in India where the month goes and the answer is nearly always the close. Reconciliations that wait on bank statements, accruals estimated from emails, intercompany balances that never quite agree, and a variance commentary written at midnight before the review meeting.

AI will not fix a close that has no process. But for a team with a reasonable checklist, it can take days out of the cycle. Here is where I would apply it, and where I would not.

## Where finance teams actually are

Gartner’s [2025 AI in Finance survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) of 183 CFOs and senior finance leaders found 59% of finance functions using AI, barely up from 58% in 2024. The most common use cases were knowledge management (49%), accounts payable process automation (37%) and error and anomaly detection (34%). Gartner also found that 91% reported low or moderate impact at first, and named data literacy and data quality as the biggest obstacles.

That matches what I see. The teams that get value from AI in the close are the ones that cleaned up their data and their checklist first.

## Where AI helps in the close

- Bank and sub-ledger reconciliations: matching at volume, with unmatched items grouped by likely cause for a person to clear.
- Accrual support: reading purchase orders, contracts and email approvals to propose accruals for services received but not invoiced, each with the supporting document attached.
- Intercompany: matching balances and transactions across entities and listing differences with the likely reason.
- Variance commentary: a first draft of the explanation for movements above a threshold, built from the ledger detail, for the controller to edit.
- Close checklist tracking: chasing owners for overdue tasks and summarising status each morning.

## Where the controller stays in charge

Estimates, judgements and anything that changes the numbers. An AI-proposed accrual is a suggestion with evidence; the controller decides whether to book it and at what amount. Variance commentary is the same: the draft explains what moved, but only someone who knows the business can say why, and whether it matters.

For listed companies this is not just good practice. Under [section 134(5)(e) of the Companies Act, 2013](https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2013/companies-act%2C-2013.pdf), the directors’ responsibility statement says the directors have laid down internal financial controls that are adequate and operating effectively, and section 143(3)(i) has the auditor report on those controls. An AI step in the close is part of that control environment and should be designed, documented and reviewed like one.

## Design the controls into the workflow

If internal audit will later test the close, it helps to build with that in mind; I set out how internal audit teams should approach AI-assisted testing in [AI for internal audit in Indian companies](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-08-ai-for-internal-audit-in-indian-companies-a-practical-starting-point).

- Every AI-generated journal proposal is labelled and requires approval by a person with the right authority.
- Reconciliation tools show the matching rule used, so a reviewer can see why two items were paired.
- Outputs are reproducible: the same inputs produce the same result, and the version of any script used is recorded.
- Exceptions are logged and reviewed weekly to find recurring causes upstream.
- Employee, customer and vendor personal data is handled under clear rules; the [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) are now notified with a phased timeline.

## Measure the close, not the tool

Before changing anything, record how many working days the close takes, how many manual journals are posted after day one, and how many review comments come back. Those are the numbers that should move. For listed companies the year-end deadline is fixed: [SEBI’s LODR FAQs](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/faqfiles/apr-2025/1745399101865.pdf) restate that audited annual results must be filed within 60 days of the end of the financial year. A faster monthly close makes that deadline much easier to meet.

Start with one area, usually bank reconciliations or accrual support, run it alongside the existing process for two closes, and only then switch. For the wider sequence, see my [AI finance automation roadmap for CFOs](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-04-ai-finance-automation-roadmap-for-cfos-and-controllers).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many finance functions use AI?

Gartner’s 2025 AI in Finance survey of 183 finance leaders found 59% of finance functions using AI, compared with 58% in 2024.

### What is the best first AI use case for the month-end close?

Bank and sub-ledger reconciliations or accrual support are good starting points: high volume, clear evidence and easy to review. Variance commentary drafts are a useful second step.

### Can AI post journal entries?

It can propose them with supporting evidence. Posting should remain subject to approval by a person with the appropriate authority, as part of the company’s internal financial controls.

### Does AI in the close affect internal financial controls?

Yes. For listed companies, directors state under section 134(5)(e) that internal financial controls are adequate and operating effectively, and the auditor reports on them under section 143(3)(i). AI steps should be designed and documented as controls.

## Sources

- [Gartner: Finance AI adoption remains steady in 2025 (press release)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025)
- [Companies Act, 2013 — Gazette text (PRS Legislative Research)](https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2013/companies-act%2C-2013.pdf)
- [SEBI: FAQs on the LODR Regulations (Regulation 33 financial results)](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/faqfiles/apr-2025/1745399101865.pdf)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)

# AI for Marketplace Seller Reconciliation in India: GST TCS and 194-O TDS

> How a CA can use AI to reconcile marketplace GST TCS and 194-O/section 393 TDS for Indian sellers before the 30 November cut-off, and what stays human.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-04-ai-for-marketplace-seller-reconciliation-in-india-gst-tcs-and-194-o-tds
Last updated: 2026-11-04

CA insights · 2026-11-04 · 7 min read

How a CA can use AI to reconcile marketplace GST TCS and 194-O/section 393 TDS for Indian sellers before the 30 November cut-off, and what stays human.

Key takeaways

- GST TCS (section 52) is 0.5 per cent of net taxable supplies from 10 July 2024; income-tax TDS on e-commerce is 0.1 per cent of gross sales.
- From 1 April 2026, section 194-O moves to section 393(1) Table serial 8(v) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, at the same 0.1 per cent.
- Sellers must accept or reject every TCS row on the GST portal before the credit reaches the electronic cash ledger.
- Operators cannot correct 2025-26 GSTR-8 errors after 30 November 2026 (or the annual statement, if earlier), so raise rejections now.
- Let AI map settlement reports and build the tie-outs; keep accept/reject decisions and tax positions with a named reviewer.

Every November a seller client rings with the same problem. The marketplace dashboard says one thing, the books say another, and in between sit months of GST TCS credit nobody accepted on the portal and income-tax TDS that does not match Form 26AS. Can AI sort it out? It can do most of the matching, and none of the deciding.

This post is for CAs and finance leads who look after Indian sellers on platforms that collect payment on the seller’s behalf. It covers the two withholding trails on every marketplace sale, where AI earns its keep, and the controls I would insist on. It is deliberately narrower than my earlier piece on [ecommerce reconciliation in general](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-20-ecommerce-reconciliation-where-automation-helps-and-where-it-lies): this one is about tax credits.

## Two trails, two bases, two portals

Most of the confusion comes from treating GST TCS and income-tax TDS as one thing. They are separate laws, calculated on different bases, reported in different returns and claimed against different liabilities.

**GST TCS under section 52 of the CGST Act.** The operator collects tax on the *net* value of taxable supplies made through it, meaning sales less returns for the month. Since 10 July 2024 the rate has been 0.5 per cent (0.25 per cent CGST plus 0.25 per cent SGST, or 0.5 per cent IGST), down from 1 per cent, under [Notification No. 15/2024–Central Tax](https://www.gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/central-tax-15-2024-11072024.pdf). The operator pays it over and files its statement in Form GSTR-8 within ten days after the end of the month, as [section 52(3) and 52(4)](https://taxinformation.cbic.gov.in/content/html/tax_repository/gst/acts/2017_CGST_act/active/chapter10/section52_v1.00.html) require.

The seller then has to act. On the GST portal, the [“TDS and TCS Credit Received” statement](https://tutorial.gst.gov.in/userguide/inputtaxcredit/manual_tds_and_tcs_credit_received.htm) shows each record the operator reported. Every row must be accepted or rejected before the statement can be filed, and accepted credit reaches the electronic cash ledger only after filing. Rejected rows flow back to the operator’s next GSTR-8 for amendment.

**Income-tax TDS on e-commerce payouts.** For the year to 31 March 2026 this is section 194-O of the 1961 Act, at 0.1 per cent of the *gross* amount of sales from 1 October 2024, after the [Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024](https://research.lawsathi.in/acts/finance-act-2024-no-2-2024/section-61/) cut it from 1 per cent. From 1 April 2026 the same deduction sits in [section 393(1), Table serial number 8(v) of the Income-tax Act, 2025](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-393-6), still at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount. Individual and HUF sellers whose gross platform sales stay within five lakh rupees in the tax year, and who have given the operator their PAN or Aadhaar, are outside it under serial number 11 of the no-deduction table in section 393(4). This credit shows up in Form 26AS and the AIS and is set against income tax, not GST; my [TDS reconciliation guide](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-13-using-ai-for-tds-reconciliation-in-indian-ca-firms-from-26as-to-form-168) covers that side in more depth.

So one sale produces a GST figure on net value and an income-tax figure on gross value. If your working paper does not separate them, the reconciliation will never close.

## Why this matters in November

Two things make this a November job rather than a March one. First, the window for correcting the operator’s side is closing. Under the proviso to section 52(6), an operator cannot rectify an omission or incorrect particulars in GSTR-8 after 30 November following the end of the financial year, or after it files the annual statement, whichever is earlier. For 2025-26 that means rejections the operator has to act on need to be raised now, not after the year-end audit. Second, the Act provides for the operator’s reported supplies to be matched against the seller’s own returns, with unresolved excess amounts added to the seller’s output liability with interest under sections 52(8) to 52(11), as the [GST Council’s e-commerce FAQ](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-02/faq-e-commerc.pdf) explains. Either way, a gap between what the platform says you sold and what you declared tends to surface later in a notice.

## Where AI genuinely helps

The work is mostly structure, which AI handles well once a person designs the template.

- **Normalising settlement reports.** Each platform labels orders, returns, commission, shipping, ads and penalties differently,. A model can map new fee lines to your chart of accounts and flag the ones it has not seen before.
- **Building the three-way tie-out.** For each GSTIN and month: platform sales and returns, the TCS rows in the portal statement, and the GSTR-1 figures. For each PAN and quarter: platform gross sales, the 194-O or section 393 credits in Form 26AS, and the TDS receivable in the books.
- **Explaining differences in plain language.** Timing (a sale in March, a return in April), base (net against gross), rate (a period straddling 10 July 2024 or 1 October 2024), wrong GSTIN on the seller account, or a genuine omission.
- **Drafting the operator query** once a person has decided a row is wrong, with order IDs and amounts attached.

## Where judgement stays human

Three decisions should never be left to a model. Accepting or rejecting a TCS row on the portal is a filing action with consequences for the cash ledger and the operator’s next return; a person who has seen the evidence clicks the button. Deciding whether a difference is timing or under-declared turnover is a tax position. And the TDS credit claimed in the income-tax return has to agree with Form 26AS and the books, with any mismatch explained by someone who signs the computation.

One data point: settlement reports carry customer names, addresses and phone numbers. Strip those columns before any upload and use a business AI plan whose retention terms a partner has read, as set out in my [DPDP rubric for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric).

Evaluation framework only. Adapt it to your practice; this is not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Task | AI role | Minimum review gate | Stop if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mapping settlement fee lines | Automate, flag new codes | Senior approves each new mapping once | Unknown codes are mapped without a flag |
| GST TCS tie-out by GSTIN and month | Automate the comparison | Every difference above your threshold has a reason | Net and gross figures are mixed in one column |
| 194-O / section 393 TDS against Form 26AS | Assist | Manager ties the total to the books and the return | The tool works from a 26AS download older than the latest quarter |
| Accept or reject TCS rows on the portal | Human only | Evidence for each rejection on file | Anyone suggests “select all” without a tie-out |
| Timing versus under-declaration | Human only | Partner or tax lead decides and documents | The model’s explanation is copied into the file as the conclusion |

## A workflow I would actually run

Start with one client and one platform. Pull twelve months of settlement reports, the portal TCS statement and the latest Form 26AS. A person writes the mapping rules on one page; the tool applies them and produces a GST table and an income-tax table with a reason column. Review the reasons, not the rows that agree. When two cycles close cleanly, add the next platform. If you are still deciding how to structure the pilot itself, the [90-day pilot guide for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india) sets out the stages.

The deliverable is a short quarterly evidence pack: both tie-outs, rejected TCS rows with reasons, operator tickets and who reviewed what. That is what you want in hand when an officer asks why the numbers differ.

## Monday-morning checklist

- List every seller client by GSTIN and PAN, with the platforms each one sells on.
- Open the “TDS and TCS Credit Received” statement for each GSTIN and note any months with unactioned rows.
- For 2025-26, list the TCS rows you expect to reject and raise them with the operator before 30 November.
- Separate GST TCS (net, section 52) from income-tax TDS (gross, section 194-O or section 393) in the working paper.
- Strip customer personal data from settlement exports before any AI tool sees them.
- Keep a log of what the tool matched, what a person changed and who signed off.

To see where this fits among the other workflows in a practice, start from the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india), or take the [free AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard) to see which reconciliation work is worth automating first. For a scoped view across a whole client book, see the [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the GST TCS rate for marketplace sellers in India?

Since 10 July 2024 an e-commerce operator collects 0.5 per cent of the net value of taxable supplies: 0.25 per cent CGST plus 0.25 per cent SGST for intra-State supplies, or 0.5 per cent IGST for inter-State supplies, under Notification No. 15/2024–Central Tax. It was 1 per cent before that date.

### Where did section 194-O go under the Income-tax Act, 2025?

From 1 April 2026, TDS by an e-commerce operator on a participant’s sales sits in section 393(1), Table serial number 8(v), at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount. Individual and HUF sellers with gross platform sales up to five lakh rupees in the tax year who have furnished PAN or Aadhaar are excluded under section 393(4). Income up to 31 March 2026 stays under section 194-O of the 1961 Act.

### Can AI accept TCS credit on the GST portal for a seller?

It should not. AI can prepare the tie-out between settlement reports and the TCS rows and suggest which rows look wrong, but accepting or rejecting a row is a filing action. A person who has reviewed the evidence should take it, because rejected rows go back to the operator and accepted credit moves to the electronic cash ledger once the statement is filed.

# Updating Engagement Letters for AI Use in a CA Firm

> Tell clients plainly how AI is used on their work, what data it sees and who reviews it. What to add to CA engagement letters now that the DPDP Rules are notified.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-11-04-updating-engagement-letters-for-ai-use-in-a-ca-firm
Last updated: 2026-11-04

CA insights · 2026-11-04 · 4 min read

Most CA firms in India now use some AI on client work, even if it is only an assistant drafting emails or summarising documents. Very few have told their clients. That gap will close one way or another: either the firm explains its approach in the engagement letter, or a client asks the question after something goes wrong.

I would rather the engagement letter answered it first. Here is what I would add, and why the timing matters.

## Why now

Two reasons. First, the [Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) were notified in November 2025, operationalising the [DPDP Act, 2023](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf) with an 18-month phased compliance timeline. Client files are full of personal data: employee payroll, customer lists, directors’ details, individual taxpayers’ records. A firm processing that data on a client’s behalf needs clarity on what it does with it.

Second, the stakes are not trivial. The [government’s explainer](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/nov/doc20251117695301.pdf) notes penalties under the Act of up to ₹250 crore for failure to maintain reasonable security safeguards, and up to ₹200 crore for failing to notify a personal data breach to the Board or affected individuals.

## Start from what SA 210 already covers

For audits, the engagement letter is governed by SA 210, and ICAI’s Auditing and Assurance Standards Board has published [illustrative engagement letters under the Companies Act, 2013](https://www.icai.org/post/aasb-illustrative-audit-engagement-letter-under-companies-act-2013-17-12-2014) that sit in Appendix 1 of the standard. AI fits naturally within the letter’s description of how the audit will be performed and how information will be handled.

For tax, advisory and bookkeeping work there is no equivalent standard letter, which is all the more reason to write the AI terms down.

## What I would add to the letter

- A plain statement that the firm uses AI tools to assist with specified tasks, such as drafting, summarising, data matching and analysis, and that professional conclusions and deliverables are reviewed and approved by named professionals.
- Which categories of client data may be processed by those tools, and which will not, for example identity documents or bank credentials.
- That tools are firm-controlled accounts with settings that stop client data being used to train public models, where the provider offers that control, and where the data is stored.
- How long data is retained in those tools, and how it is deleted at the end of the engagement.
- How the firm will inform the client of a security incident affecting their data, and the contact person for data questions.
- A route for the client to ask that AI not be used on their work, and what that means for fees and timelines.

## Make sure the firm can keep the promises

An engagement letter that describes controls the firm does not have is worse than silence. Before the clause goes out, check that it matches reality: which tools are approved, who has access, where data sits, what the retention settings are and who reviews outputs. My [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india) is a reasonable place to start.

Internal auditors now have a useful test for this in ICAI’s [SIA 240](https://internalaudit.icai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Comp-of-Stnd-on-Internal-Audit-26.pdf), which asks that tools comply with data privacy and cybersecurity rules and that third-party tools have adequate confidentiality, ownership and access controls. It names the DPDP Act, 2023 directly. The same questions work for any practice.

## Talk to clients, not just send the letter

Most clients react well to a short conversation: we use these tools for these tasks, a professional reviews everything, your data stays in these systems. What worries clients is finding out later. I would also brief the team, so that whoever answers a client’s question about AI gives the same answer the letter does. If you have not yet chosen the assistant itself, I compared the main options in [ChatGPT vs Copilot vs Gemini for a CA firm](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-05-chatgpt-vs-copilot-vs-gemini-how-a-ca-firm-in-india-should-choose-an-ai-assistant).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do CA firms need to tell clients they use AI?

There is no single rule requiring a specific disclosure, but engagement terms should describe how client information is handled, and the DPDP framework places obligations on entities processing personal data. Stating AI use in the engagement letter avoids surprises; take advice on your own facts.

### When do the DPDP Rules apply?

The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline, according to the government’s press release.

### What should an AI clause in an engagement letter cover?

The tasks AI assists with, who reviews outputs, which data the tools may process, where data is stored and for how long, how incidents will be notified, and how a client can opt out.

### Does SA 210 mention AI?

SA 210 and ICAI’s illustrative engagement letters predate generative AI and do not address it specifically. AI use fits within the letter’s description of how the audit will be performed and how information will be handled.

## Sources

- [ICAI AASB: Illustrative engagement letters under the Companies Act, 2013 (SA 210, Appendix 1)](https://www.icai.org/post/aasb-illustrative-audit-engagement-letter-under-companies-act-2013-17-12-2014)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)
- [PIB: DPDP Rules, 2025 explainer (penalties under the DPDP Act, 2023)](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/nov/doc20251117695301.pdf)
- [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Gazette text, MeitY)](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf)
- [ICAI Internal Audit Standards Board: Compendium of Standards on Internal Audit, 2026 (SIA 240, Use of Tools)](https://internalaudit.icai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Comp-of-Stnd-on-Internal-Audit-26.pdf)

# AI Prompts for Bank Reconciliation: What Works and What to Check

> Prompts for bank reconciliation with Claude or ChatGPT, written by a CA: file preparation, matching rules, outputs to request and the checks before you post.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-30-ai-prompts-for-bank-reconciliation-what-works-and-what-to-check
Last updated: 2026-10-30

AI automation · 2026-10-30 · 4 min read

Bank reconciliation is one of the first jobs people try with AI, and “AI prompt for bank reconciliation” is a growing search. Most of what you find is a single prompt in a social post: upload the statement and the ledger, ask the model to match them, done. It often works on a clean demo month. It often fails quietly on a real one.

Here is how I would prompt for bank reconciliation so that the output is something an accountant can review and stand behind.

## Prepare the files before you prompt

Structured data makes everything easier. Consent-based Account Aggregator feeds are one route; [Sahamati](https://sahamati.org.in/media-article/account-aggregator-crosses-500-million-consents-as-india-marks-5th-aa-foundation-day/) reports the network has crossed 500 million consents. Where a client’s bank supports it, a structured feed beats a downloaded PDF.

- Bank statement as CSV or Excel, not PDF where you can avoid it; one row per transaction with date, narration, reference, debit, credit and balance.
- Bank ledger export from the accounting system for the same period, plus the closing balance per books.
- The previous month’s unreconciled items, so carried-forward cheques and deposits are not treated as new.
- Remove columns the matching does not need, especially personal details in narrations where possible.

## A prompt structure that holds up

I write reconciliation prompts in five parts. Describe each file and its columns. State the matching rules in order: exact amount and reference first, then exact amount within three days, then exact amount only, each as a separate pass. List the outputs you want. Add the rules the model must not break. Finally, ask it to show its counts so you can check nothing was dropped.

The rules matter most. I always include: do not create entries to force the balance to agree; do not match one bank line to more than one ledger line unless I ask; list every line you could not classify; and keep the original row numbers so I can trace each match.

## Outputs to ask for

- Matched items, with the pass on which each was matched.
- In bank, not in books: charges, interest, direct credits, returned cheques.
- In books, not in bank: unpresented cheques and deposits in transit, with their age.
- Possible duplicates on either side.
- A reconciliation statement from the bank balance to the book balance, with totals that tie.

## Checks before you post anything

- Tie the opening and closing balances in the model’s statement to the actual bank statement and ledger.
- Check the row counts: matched plus unmatched should equal the total on each side.
- Review every match from the looser passes; amount-only matches are where errors hide.
- Investigate old unpresented items rather than carrying them forward again.
- Post adjusting entries yourself, after review; do not let the tool post directly.

## Where the time really goes

In my experience the matching is rarely the slow part. Chasing unexplained receipts, missing narrations and duplicate entries is. AI helps most when it hands you a short, well-organised exceptions list on day one of the close. Anomaly detection is one of the most common finance AI uses in [Gartner’s 2025 survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025), which fits what I see in practice.

For the broader close, my [AI finance automation roadmap](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-04-ai-finance-automation-roadmap-for-cfos-and-controllers) sets out what to automate in what order.

## Data and access

Bank statements reveal salaries, customers, suppliers and personal payments. The [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) were notified in November 2025 with a phased timeline. Use a business AI account with training on your data turned off, keep files in company storage, and record which tool processed which statement.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can ChatGPT or Claude do a bank reconciliation?

They can match transactions and produce an exceptions list and reconciliation statement from clean CSV files. An accountant should check balances, row counts and loose matches, and post any entries after review.

### What should a bank reconciliation prompt include?

A description of each file, matching rules in order of strictness, the outputs you want, rules such as not creating entries to force agreement, and a request for row counts so nothing is silently dropped.

### Should AI post reconciliation entries automatically?

Not without review. Let the tool propose adjusting entries and post them yourself after checking, so every change to the books has an accountable approver.

### Is it safe to upload bank statements to AI tools?

Only to an approved business account with training on your data turned off and retention settings checked. Remove unnecessary personal details and record which tool processed which file.

## Sources

- [Sahamati: Account Aggregator crosses 500 million consents (2 September 2026)](https://sahamati.org.in/media-article/account-aggregator-crosses-500-million-consents-as-india-marks-5th-aa-foundation-day/)
- [Gartner: Finance AI adoption remains steady in 2025 (press release)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)

# AI for CA Students: Using ChatGPT and CA GPT Without Weakening Your Prep

> A practising CA’s guide for CA students: where ChatGPT and ICAI’s CA GPT help exam prep, where they mislead, and the habits that build real exam skill.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-29-ai-for-ca-students-using-chatgpt-and-ca-gpt-without-weakening-your-prep
Last updated: 2026-10-29

CA insights · 2026-10-29 · 4 min read

CA students are using AI whether firms and coaching classes like it or not. On student forums the same complaint keeps appearing: the chatbot sounded confident, the answer was wrong, and the student only found out in a mock test. Search results for “ChatGPT for CA students” are mostly forum threads and short videos, with very little structured advice.

I am a CA and I now help firms adopt AI. This is what I would tell a student about using it for preparation, honestly and without hype.

## The exam has not got easier

In the [CA Final May 2026 result](https://www.icai.org/post/prc-caresult-may2026), 14.07% of candidates who appeared in both groups passed: 3,345 out of 23,776. Group I was 12% and Group II 20.49%. Those numbers are a reminder that the exam tests applied judgement under time pressure. A tool that hands you finished answers can make you feel prepared while weakening exactly that skill.

The healthy way to use AI is the way a good senior uses a junior: to save time on the mechanical parts while doing the thinking yourself. If the tool does the thinking, the gap only shows in the exam hall, where there is no chatbot and the question has a twist you have never practised.

## Where AI genuinely helps a student

- Explaining a concept a second way when the study material is not landing.
- Turning your own notes into flashcards and quick revision questions.
- Building a study timetable around articleship hours and exam dates.
- Checking the structure of a written answer you have already attempted.
- Practising viva-style questions on a topic before group study.

## Where it misleads

General chatbots are weakest exactly where CA exams are strictest: current tax rates and provisions, amendments, section numbers, and computational questions with several adjustments. They also tend to give an answer rather than say “it depends”, which is the opposite of how examiners reward reasoning. Treat any figure, section or case name from a general chatbot as unverified until you have found it in ICAI material.

ICAI’s own [CA GPT](https://ai.icai.org/cagpt/) is built on institute content and is a safer starting point for students than a general tool. It is still a study aid, not a replacement for the study material, RTPs and MTPs.

## Habits that build exam skill

- Attempt first, ask second: write your answer before asking any tool, then compare.
- Ask the tool to find errors in your answer rather than to write one.
- Verify every number and provision against the study material for your attempt.
- Keep a log of the tool’s mistakes; it trains your scepticism, which the profession needs.
- Never paste confidential client data from articleship into a personal chatbot.

## Articleship is where AI skills count

Under the new scheme, practical training lasts two years, according to ICAI’s [FAQs on the New Scheme of Education and Training](https://resource.cdn.icai.org/75315bos-faqs-nset-july1.pdf). That is when you will meet AI tools in real work: reconciliations, working papers, notice drafts. Firms will value article assistants who can review machine output critically, not just operate the tool. My piece on [how CA firms should train article assistants](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-15-ai-and-articleship-how-ca-firms-should-train-article-assistants-now) covers the firm’s side.

## The skills employers will look for

The World Economic Forum’s [Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/in-full/3-skills-outlook/) expects 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, with AI and big data the fastest-growing skills. For a newly qualified CA, that means comfort with AI tools plus the judgement to know when they are wrong. If you are weighing the qualification itself, read [is CA worth it in 2026 with AI](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-is-ca-worth-it-in-2026-with-ai).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is ChatGPT useful for CA exam preparation?

Yes, for explaining concepts, revision questions, timetables and reviewing answers you have already written. It is unreliable for current tax provisions, section numbers and multi-step computations, so verify everything against ICAI material.

### What is ICAI CA GPT?

An AI platform from ICAI built on institute content, available to members and students through the ICAI AI portal. It is a safer starting point than a general chatbot but is still a study aid.

### How hard is CA Final now?

In the May 2026 CA Final, 14.07% of candidates who appeared in both groups passed (3,345 of 23,776), according to ICAI’s result press release.

### Can I use AI during articleship work?

Only with your principal’s approval and the firm’s approved tools. Never paste client data into a personal chatbot account, and always review the output before it goes into a working paper.

### Should CA students learn AI tools?

Yes. Articleship and early jobs increasingly involve reviewing AI output, and the WEF expects AI and big data to be the fastest-growing skills to 2030. Learn the tools and the habit of checking them.

## Sources

- [ICAI Board of Studies: FAQs on the New Scheme of Education and Training](https://resource.cdn.icai.org/75315bos-faqs-nset-july1.pdf)

# AI Automation Agency vs Consultant in India: How to Choose

> Hiring help for AI automation in India? When an agency fits, when an independent consultant fits, and the questions to ask either before signing anything.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-28-ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant-in-india-how-to-choose
Last updated: 2026-10-28

AI automation · 2026-10-28 · 4 min read

“AI automation agency India” and “AI automation consultant India” are now common searches, and the results are mostly agencies writing about why you should hire an agency. I am an independent consultant, so read this knowing my bias. I have tried to write the guide I would want if I were the buyer.

The honest answer is that both models work, for different jobs. What matters more is how you scope the work and what you insist on owning at the end.

## Why the decision matters now

Demand is not the issue. Microsoft’s [2025 Work Trend Index findings for India](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2025/08/20/indias-workforce-goes-ai-first-as-frontier-firms-lead-the-transformation-microsoft-work-trend-index-2025/) report that 93% of Indian leaders intend to use AI agents to extend workforce capacity in the next 12 to 18 months. The risk is buying delivery before you know which workflow is worth automating, or ending up with automations nobody in the business can maintain.

There are two common ways this goes wrong. A business pays for many builds that are not tied to any metric, so nobody can say later which ones earned their keep. Or it buys a roadmap with nobody to build or run anything, so the plan sits in a folder. The model you hire should match the gap you actually have: knowing what to automate, or having the hands to build it.

## When an agency fits

- You already know the workflows and need several built, integrated and supported in production.
- You need a team: developers, an integration specialist and someone to monitor and fix things.
- You want a support contract with response times, and you have budget for ongoing fees.
- Your own IT team can review the architecture and hold the agency to it.

## When an independent consultant fits

- You are not yet sure where AI pays back and need the workflows mapped, ranked and costed first.
- The work touches finance, controls or regulated data, and you want someone who understands the process as well as the tools.
- You need one narrow release designed and run alongside the old process before committing to more.
- You want help writing the brief and evaluating agencies or vendors, without a stake in who wins.

## Questions to ask either one

- Show me a system you built that is still running in production, and let me speak to the client.
- Who exactly will do the work, and who will maintain it after go-live?
- What baseline will we measure before we start, and what number should move?
- Who owns the code, prompts, workflows, credentials and documentation at the end?
- Where will our data be processed and stored, and is any of it used to train models?
- What happens if we stop the engagement: what do we receive, and in what format?

## Governance is part of the scope

Whoever you hire should design controls in from the start, not add them later. MeitY’s [India AI Governance Guidelines](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639) favour a principles-based approach built on existing laws, with accountability and human oversight proportionate to risk, and the [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) bring a phased timeline for personal data duties. The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) is a useful neutral checklist: govern, map, measure, manage. If a proposal does not mention data access, logging, approval steps and an owner for each automation, ask why.

## A sensible way to buy

Start with a short, paid discovery that ends in a ranked list of workflows, a baseline and one designed release. Run that release with one team for a few weeks. Only then sign a larger build or support contract, with the evidence in hand. This is roughly how I structure the [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), and it is a fair way to test any provider, including me.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I hire an AI agency or a consultant in India?

Hire an agency when you know the workflows and need several built and supported in production. Hire an independent consultant when you first need the workflows mapped, ranked and one release designed and tested, especially where finance or regulated data is involved.

### What should an AI automation contract include?

A measured baseline, named people, ownership of code, prompts and documentation, data processing terms, support arrangements and what you receive if the engagement ends.

### Do Indian AI governance rules affect automation projects?

MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines are principles-based and rely on existing laws, and the DPDP Rules, 2025 set a phased timeline for personal data duties. Both mean controls and data handling should be in scope from the start.

### How do I test an AI provider before a big commitment?

Buy a short paid discovery and one narrow release run alongside your current process, then decide on a larger contract based on the measured result.

## Sources

- [PIB: MeitY unveils the India AI Governance Guidelines (5 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)
- [Microsoft: India findings of the 2025 Work Trend Index](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2025/08/20/indias-workforce-goes-ai-first-as-frontier-firms-lead-the-transformation-microsoft-work-trend-index-2025/)
- [NIST: AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

# AI for AOC-4 and MGT-7 Filings: What a CA Can Automate Before the ROC Deadline

> How a CA firm can use AI to tie AOC-4 to signed accounts and build MGT-7 data before the section 137 and 92 deadlines, and what stays human.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-28-ai-for-aoc-4-and-mgt-7-filings-what-a-ca-can-automate-before-the-roc-deadline
Last updated: 2026-10-28

CA insights · 2026-10-28 · 6 min read

How a CA firm can use AI to tie AOC-4 to signed accounts and build MGT-7 data before the section 137 and 92 deadlines, and what stays human.

Key takeaways

- AOC-4 is due within thirty days of the AGM under section 137, and MGT-7 within sixty days under section 92(4).
- AI is best used to compare form data with the signed accounts and to build shareholding, director and meeting tables with a source on every row.
- Reasons for not holding an AGM, penalties, compounding, MGT-8 certification and the digital signature stay with people.
- Late annual returns attract ten thousand rupees plus one hundred rupees a day, capped at two lakh rupees for the company.
- Build the master data once for AOC-4 and reuse it for MGT-7, and keep client identifiers inside a firm-managed business AI account.

Late October is when the ROC season stops being theoretical. Most companies with a 31 March year-end held their AGMs by the end of September, which puts AOC-4 and MGT-7 on the same desk as tax audit follow-ups and the first GST notices of the half-year. Firms are now asking me a reasonable question: can AI take some of this load without putting a wrong number on a public record?

It can, if you are strict about where it sits. ROC filings are a good fit for AI because most of the work is carrying data that already exists from one document into another and checking that it matches. They are a bad fit for AI wherever the filing records a judgement or a certification. Below is how I draw that line, with the statutory dates the workflow has to respect.

## The dates the workflow is built around

Three sections of the Companies Act, 2013 set the clock, and every AI step below should be planned backwards from them.

- **The AGM.** Under [section 96](https://ca2013.com/annual-general-meeting/), an AGM after the first must be held within a period of six months from the close of the financial year (subject to the other conditions in the section and any extension granted).
- **Financial statements (AOC-4).** [Section 137](https://ca2013.com/137-copy-of-financial-statement-to-be-filed-with-registrar/) requires the adopted financial statements, with the attached documents, to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the AGM. Unadopted statements go in within the same thirty days and are taken on record as provisional.
- **Annual return (MGT-7 or MGT-7A).** [Section 92(4)](https://indiacode.ecourtsindia.com/companies-act/section/92/) gives sixty days from the AGM, or from the date it should have been held. Section 92(5) sets a penalty of ten thousand rupees for failure, plus one hundred rupees a day while it continues, capped at two lakh rupees for the company and fifty thousand rupees for an officer in default.

So for a company whose AGM was on 30 September, AOC-4 falls due at the end of October and MGT-7 about a month later. That gap matters. It means you can use AI for the AOC-4 tie-out now and reuse the same extracted master data for the annual return, instead of keying the shareholding and director details twice.

## Where AI earns its place in ROC work

The useful jobs are all variations of “read, extract, compare, list the differences”.

- **Tying the form to the signed accounts.** Give the tool the signed financial statements and the draft AOC-4 data and ask for a line-by-line comparison: every figure, with the page and note it came from. A person then checks only the mismatches and the figures the tool could not locate.
- **Building the master data once.** Shareholding pattern, transfers during the year, directors and KMP with appointment and cessation dates, meeting dates and attendance. These come from registers, minutes and earlier filings. AI is quick at pulling them into one table with a source reference against each row.
- **Cross-checking the board’s report.** [Section 134](https://ca2013.com/134-financial-statement-boards-report-etc/) lists what the board’s report must contain. A checklist run, with the tool marking each required matter as present, absent or unclear, is a fast first review before the partner reads it properly.
- **Year-on-year consistency.** Comparing this year’s draft against last year’s filed forms catches the dull errors: a changed CIN typo, a director still listed after resignation, a share count that does not roll forward.
- **The filing tracker.** For a firm with many companies, a tracker that reads AGM dates and computes the section 137 and section 92 deadlines, then flags anything missing, is the least glamorous and most valuable automation on this list. The arithmetic is simple; the value is that nobody has to remember.

## What stays with people

Anything that is a judgement, a declaration or a certification stays human, and the tool should not be allowed to fill it in “helpfully”.

- Whether the financial statements were adopted, and the treatment if they were not.
- The reasons statement where no AGM was held. That is the company’s explanation, not a template.
- Penalties, compounding and related-party disclosures in the annual return, which need the facts from management and the legal file.
- Certification. The annual return of a listed company, or one above the prescribed paid-up capital or turnover, must be certified by a company secretary in practice in MGT-8. The [ICSI guidance note on the annual return](https://www.icsi.edu/media/webmodules/publications/A29ChapterPages.pdf) sets the thresholds out as paid-up capital of ten crore rupees or turnover of fifty crore rupees. A certifying professional has to form their own view from the records; a model summary is not evidence.
- The digital signature. No workflow should store or apply a DSC on anyone’s behalf.

## A decision table for ROC filings

I use the same structure as the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework): map the task, decide the AI role, set the review gate and agree when to stop.

Evaluation framework only. Adapt it to your practice; this is not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Task | AI role | Minimum review gate | Stop if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deadline tracker from AGM dates | Automate | Manager checks AGM dates against minutes once | AGM dates taken from email rather than minutes |
| AOC-4 figures against signed accounts | Automate the comparison | Article clerk or senior clears every mismatch | Tool compares against an unsigned draft |
| Shareholding, directors and meetings table | Assist | Each row traced to a register or minute | Rows without a source reference |
| Board’s report checklist under section 134 | Assist | Partner reads the report in full | The checklist replaces the read |
| Reasons for not holding an AGM, penalties, compounding | Human only | Facts confirmed by management in writing | Any text drafted from a template without facts |
| MGT-8 certification | Human only | Practising CS forms an independent view | Certification relies on a model summary |

## Client data before the first upload

ROC files carry personal data: director PAN and DIN details, addresses and shareholder lists. Use a business AI plan whose retention and training terms a partner has actually read, mask identifiers the task does not need, and keep the extraction inside a firm-managed account. The same reasoning I set out for [DPDP and AI in CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric) applies here: decide your role on the engagement, then decide what the tool may see.

## Monday-morning checklist

- List every company whose AGM was held, and the date, from the minutes.
- Compute the section 137 and section 92 due dates and sort the list by the nearer one.
- Run the AOC-4 tie-out against signed accounts only; clear the mismatch list the same day.
- Build the master data table once, with a source against every row, and reuse it for MGT-7.
- Mark the human-only fields in each form before anyone opens the tool.
- Keep a short log: what the tool compared, what a person changed, who signed off.

If you want to see where this sits among the other workflows in a practice, start from the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india), or take the [free AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard) to see which compliance work is worth automating first.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI file AOC-4 or MGT-7 for a company?

AI can prepare and cross-check the data, for example by comparing AOC-4 figures with the signed financial statements and building the shareholding and director tables for MGT-7. The filing, declarations, certification and digital signature remain the responsibility of the company and its professionals.

### What is the due date for AOC-4 and MGT-7?

Under section 137 of the Companies Act, 2013, financial statements are filed within thirty days of the AGM. Under section 92(4), the annual return is filed within sixty days of the AGM, or of the date it should have been held. Check MCA circulars for any extension.

### What is the penalty for filing MGT-7 late?

Section 92(5) sets a penalty of ten thousand rupees, plus one hundred rupees for each day the failure continues, up to two lakh rupees for the company and fifty thousand rupees for an officer in default.
